guides.explanation_en: 大 means great in size or importance, and 事 means a matter or undertaking. Together, 大事 is a matter of great importance or scale—an important undertaking.

国家 is the conventional word for a country or nation understood as a political community. 国 points to the country or polity; 家’s contribution to the whole is not fully predictable from its usual sense of “home” or “household.”
guides.caveat_en: Do not interpret 国家 as a literal “country-household”; it functions as a conventional word for a nation or country.

parts.contribution_en: part of the conventional word; its usual sense of “home” or “household” does not fully explain the whole

guides.explanation_en: 钱 names money: value used for payment and exchange. It refers to money as a whole, with no meaningful smaller part to explain in this word.
他们 combines the third-person pronoun 他 with 们, which marks a group of people. It means “they” or “them”; the sentence determines its grammatical role, and the group can be mixed-gender.
guides.caveat_en: In writing, 她们 is commonly used for a group of women; both forms are pronounced tāmen.

parts.contribution_en: Marks the pronoun as referring to a group.

guides.explanation_en: 在 marks a place as the location where an action happens. It links the action to where it takes place, like “at” or “in” in English.
喝酒 means to drink alcohol. 喝 names the action, and 酒 identifies what is drunk.

parts.contribution_en: Alcoholic drink, the object of the drinking.

guides.explanation_en: 大家 is the conventional word for everyone or everybody in a group. 家 can suggest a household or group of people, but the whole meaning is established and cannot be worked out precisely as “big household.”
guides.caveat_en: The everyday meaning “everyone” is conventional; the parts do not define exactly which people are included.

parts.contribution_en: part of the established word; it does not simply mean “big” in this expression
can suggest a household or group, but does not independently mean “everyone”

guides.explanation_en: After a number, 多 indicates that the amount exceeds that number. With a count, it means “more than” the stated amount.
还 adds something to what has already been mentioned, signaling that it too is included or happens in addition. It modifies the statement rather than naming the added item.

parts.contribution_en: Signals that something is also included or happens in addition.

guides.explanation_en: 事 refers broadly to a matter, affair, or undertaking—something that happens or is dealt with. By itself, it does not say what the matter involves.
听 means “hear” or “listen to”: it can refer to perceiving sound or attending to what someone says. It is a single word, not a combination of smaller words.

一起 means that people or things act or occur together, as part of the same activity or situation. The word functions as a whole; its conventional meaning is not reliably derived by adding the separate meanings of 一 and 起.
guides.caveat_en: Do not read 起 here as independently meaning “together”; the word’s ordinary meaning is lexicalized.

guides.explanation_en: 送来 combines sending or delivering something with 来, which directs the movement toward the relevant destination. The result is that the item is sent or brought to that place.

parts.contribution_en: Directs the movement toward the relevant destination.

guides.explanation_en: 村里 means within the area of a village. 村 names the village, and 里 locates something inside or within it; the phrase can refer to the village's interior or its local area.
坐 means to sit, and 下 adds the change into a seated position. Together, 坐下 means to sit down or take a seat.

parts.contribution_en: marks the change into the seated position

guides.explanation_en: 找来 means to find people and bring them toward a relevant place or person. 找 supplies the act of locating them; 来 adds movement toward a reference point, so the phrase describes finding them and getting them there.

parts.contribution_en: add movement toward a relevant reference point

guides.explanation_en: 可是 is a conventional linking word meaning “but” or “however.” It signals that what follows contrasts with or qualifies what came before.
guides.caveat_en: The contrast meaning belongs to 可是 as a whole; the separate meanings of 可 and 是 do not explain it.

guides.explanation_en: 剑 means “sword,” a bladed weapon. It is a single word and is not usefully divided into smaller meaningful parts.
When said of a flower, 开 means to open into bloom. It describes flowering, rather than simply being open.

parts.contribution_en: Means to bloom when said of a flower.

guides.explanation_en: 个 is a general classifier used when counting people or things. It supplies a counting unit without specifying a special shape or category.
和 links coordinated nouns, meaning “and.” It connects the nouns as items in the same phrase and is not usefully divided into smaller meaningful parts.
拜 is a verb for carrying out a formal rite or ritual act. What follows can identify the rite's focus or participants.
guides.caveat_en: 拜 is a single verb here; its ritual meaning is not built from smaller meaningful parts.

parts.contribution_en: perform a formal rite or ritual act

guides.explanation_en: 二哥 is a kinship term for the second elder brother in a sibling order. 二 gives the position, and 哥 means an older brother.
guides.caveat_en: The position is understood relative to the family or sibling group; the term is not necessarily a personal name.

parts.contribution_en: the second position in sibling order

guides.explanation_en: 问 describes putting a question to someone, typically to seek information or an answer. The character names the act of asking as a whole.

parts.contribution_en: Describes putting a question to someone.

guides.explanation_en: 这里 combines 这, “this,” with 里, which contributes the sense of a place or location. Together they point to the place being referred to: “here” or “this place.”

parts.contribution_en: Points to the place being referred to.

guides.explanation_en: 招兵 means to recruit soldiers. 招 describes calling for or enlisting people, and 兵 names the soldiers being recruited.
关羽 is the personal name Guan Yu, used to identify a particular person.
guides.caveat_en: The characters function together as a name; their separate meanings do not explain the person's identity or the name's origin.

guides.explanation_en: 乡勇 refers to locally based fighters, often a local militia. 乡 locates them in a local or rural community, while 勇 refers to the men as fighters; together they name a group of local armed men.
guides.caveat_en: 勇 contributes to the conventional label for the fighters; it does not mean that each person’s bravery is being asserted.

guides.explanation_en: 人 means a human being, either one person or people collectively. The word itself does not specify identity or number.

parts.contribution_en: A human being or human beings collectively.

guides.explanation_en: 大 marks the eldest or senior position among brothers, and 哥 means brother. Together, 大哥 refers to an eldest brother or a senior brother.
guides.caveat_en: As a form of address, 大哥 can refer to a senior brother without identifying someone’s eldest biological brother.

parts.contribution_en: marks the eldest or senior position

guides.explanation_en: 同一 means “the same” or “one and the same.” 同 marks sameness, while 一 presents what is shared as one and the same thing or identity.

parts.contribution_en: One, framing what is shared as a single thing or identity.

guides.explanation_en: 第二天 means the second day in an ordered sequence, commonly the day after a point of reference. 第 marks an ordinal, 二 supplies “two,” and 天 means “day.”
guides.caveat_en: Which day counts as the second depends on the sequence or reference point.

guides.explanation_en: 天 means heaven or sky, and 地 means earth or ground. Together, 天地 names heaven and earth as a whole, which may be invoked as witnesses in a traditional oath or wedding rite.
guides.caveat_en: The ritual use comes from the practice of invoking heaven and earth; 天地 itself does not mean “wedding.”

guides.explanation_en: 怎么 is an interrogative asking about the manner or nature of a situation. Depending on what is being asked, it can mean “how?” or “what?”
guides.caveat_en: It functions as a conventional whole; the individual characters do not give a dependable breakdown of its interrogative meaning.

guides.explanation_en: 高兴 means feeling happy or pleased. 高 adds an elevated, positive quality to 兴, which contributes the sense of mood or spirits; together they describe a cheerful state of mind.
guides.caveat_en: The word conventionally means happy or pleased; it does not imply literal height or a particular cause for the feeling.

parts.contribution_en: Contributes the sense of mood or spirits.

guides.explanation_en: 后来 is a conventional time word meaning “later” or “afterward” in a sequence. 后 points to what is after; together the word locates a subsequent time.
guides.caveat_en: 来 is not a literal act of coming in this time expression.

parts.contribution_en: After or subsequent in a sequence.
Part of the conventional expression for a later point in time; it does not describe physical movement.

guides.explanation_en: 看 can mean directing one's eyes toward something, or perceiving it as a result. The surrounding wording makes clear whether the focus is on looking or on seeing and noticing.
也 adds a person, thing, or point to what is already included: it means that this one is included as well, or that the same statement applies too.
来 means to come toward a speaker or another reference point. With an action, it can also assign that action to someone as the person who will do it or take a turn doing it.
guides.caveat_en: The motion meaning and the action-taking function are distinct uses of this same word.

parts.contribution_en: come toward a reference point; with an action, take it on or take a turn doing it

guides.explanation_en: After a verb, 得 introduces a complement that describes the action or its degree. The phrase after 得 supplies that description, such as how an action is carried out or how it appears.

parts.contribution_en: Links a verb to a following descriptive or degree complement.

guides.explanation_en: 叹气 means “sigh.” 叹 describes sighing or lamenting, and 气 refers to breath, so together they name the breath released in a sigh.

parts.contribution_en: Breath, as part of the act of sighing.

guides.explanation_en: 告示 is a notice or public announcement. 告 contributes telling or informing, and 示 contributes showing or making something known; together they refer to information made known to others.
件 is a classifier that counts a matter or event as one item, as in 一件事, “one matter.”

parts.contribution_en: Classifies a matter or event as a countable item.

guides.explanation_en: 五十 means fifty: 五 counts five groups, and 十 supplies the unit of ten. Together they form five tens.
推 means to push something by applying force so that it moves. The movement may be away from the person pushing or onward in a direction.

parts.contribution_en: apply force to move something by pushing

guides.explanation_en: 都 applies a statement to every member of a group. It gathers the people or things under discussion as a whole and indicates that none are left out.

parts.contribution_en: Marks the statement as applying to every member of the group.

guides.explanation_en: 两 gives the quantity two, commonly before a classifier or noun to count people or things.
进 describes movement into a place or space. The movement reaches the inside, rather than stopping at an approach toward it.

parts.contribution_en: Describes movement into a place or space.

guides.explanation_en: 三人 means a group of three people. 三 gives the number, and 人 identifies the members being counted; context can make the group specific.
穿上 means to put clothing or armor on so that it ends up being worn. 穿 supplies the action of putting on, and 上 marks the resulting state of having it on.

parts.contribution_en: marks the result: the item is on and being worn

guides.explanation_en: 请 means to ask or invite someone to do something, often politely. The requested action can be framed as a request or as an invitation, depending on context.

parts.contribution_en: ask or invite someone to do something, often politely

guides.explanation_en: 打仗 means to fight a war or go to battle. 打 is the fighting action, and 仗 is the battle or war being fought, so together they refer to engaging in warfare.

parts.contribution_en: The battle or war that is fought.

guides.explanation_en: 桃园 is a garden or orchard where peach trees grow. 桃 identifies the kind of trees, and 园 names the cultivated place they grow in.

parts.contribution_en: peach; identifies the trees grown there
garden or orchard; the place where they grow

guides.explanation_en: 的 links a describing phrase to the noun it modifies, marking what kind of thing it is or which thing is meant. The phrase before 的 supplies the description; 的 connects it to the noun.

parts.contribution_en: links a modifier or describing phrase to the noun it describes

guides.explanation_en: 他 is a third-person pronoun, commonly translated as “he” or “him” in writing. Its role as subject or object comes from the sentence; in speech, tā does not distinguish gender.
guides.caveat_en: Written Chinese commonly uses 他 for a male person; 她 is the usual written form for a woman. The spoken pronouns have the same pronunciation.

parts.contribution_en: A third-person pronoun referring to a person.

guides.explanation_en: 客 means guest or visitor, and 人 means person. Together, 客人 means a person who visits or is received as a guest.
铁 names the metal iron. It refers to the material as a whole, with no meaningful smaller part to explain in this word.
有 can present something as possessed by or available to someone, or as existing in a place or situation. With a number or group, it can also describe ending up with that amount.
guides.caveat_en: The subject and context determine whether 有 expresses possession, existence, or a resulting amount.

parts.contribution_en: express possession, existence, or having a resulting amount

guides.explanation_en: 盔甲 means armor worn for protection. 盔 refers especially to a helmet, while 甲 refers to armor; together they name protective gear broadly rather than requiring both a helmet and body armor.
guides.caveat_en: The parts evoke types of protective gear, but the word does not specify a particular set or design of armor.

guides.explanation_en: 做 broadly means to do or carry something out. With something to be produced as its object, it means “make”; with a role or relationship, it can mean “become” or “take on” that role.
guides.caveat_en: The meaning depends on what follows: 做 does not mean “become” with every kind of object.

parts.contribution_en: A verb for carrying out an action; with the right object, producing something or taking on a role.

guides.explanation_en: 张飞 is the personal name Zhang Fei, a character in Romance of the Three Kingdoms. The characters function together as a name, rather than describing the person through their ordinary meanings.
guides.caveat_en: The name's characters do not by themselves explain its origin or the person who bears it.

parts.contribution_en: The complete personal name, read Zhang Fei.

guides.explanation_en: 去 means “go” or “go to.” Before an action, it can describe going somewhere to do that action, as in going to help.
着, pronounced zhe, marks an action or state as continuing, often while another event occurs. It presents the action or state as ongoing rather than as a completed event.
guides.caveat_en: This explanation covers 着 pronounced zhe as an aspect particle; the character also has other readings and uses.

parts.contribution_en: marks an ongoing action or state

guides.explanation_en: 五百 means five hundred: 五 counts five groups, and 百 supplies the unit of one hundred. Together they form five hundreds.
你 is the second-person pronoun for the person being addressed. It can mean “you” as subject or object, and context can allow it to address more than one person.

parts.contribution_en: The second-person pronoun for the addressee.

guides.explanation_en: 马 is the ordinary word for a horse. It is a single meaningful unit, not a word made from smaller parts.
所以 connects a reason or preceding circumstance to its consequence, meaning “so” or “therefore.” It works as a connective with this meaning as a whole.
guides.caveat_en: The characters do not transparently explain this connective meaning, so it is best learned as a whole word.

guides.explanation_en: 店 means a shop or store, a place where goods or services are offered for sale.
救人 means to rescue or save people from danger or harm. 救 names the act of helping someone out of danger, and 人 identifies who is being helped.

parts.contribution_en: rescue or save from danger or harm

guides.explanation_en: 两人 means two people considered as a group. 两 gives the number, and 人 tells what is being counted; the phrase can refer to a particular pair when context identifies them.
明天 means tomorrow, the day after today. 天 contributes “day,” while 明 has a conventional temporal sense of the coming or next day in this expression.
guides.caveat_en: The meaning “tomorrow” is conventional; 明 does not mean “bright” in this word.

parts.contribution_en: the coming or next day in this time expression

guides.explanation_en: 车 names a wheeled vehicle; in this sense, it is a cart used to carry people or goods. The word refers to the vehicle as a whole.

parts.contribution_en: Names a wheeled vehicle, including a cart.

guides.explanation_en: 了 can present an action as completed or viewed as a whole. It can also mark a resulting, changed, or newly reached state, including a state that has newly come into existence. The surrounding construction determines which reading applies.
guides.caveat_en: 了 does not always mean simply “finished”; its aspectual and state-marking uses depend on the sentence.

guides.explanation_en: 是 links a subject with an identity or category, saying that the subject is or counts as what follows. It expresses a relation rather than an action.

parts.contribution_en: link a subject to an identity or classification

guides.explanation_en: 到 means to reach or arrive at a place. After a verb such as 看, it marks reaching the result of that action: 看到了 means that the seeing succeeded, or that someone saw something.
guides.caveat_en: The result-complement use depends on a preceding verb; 到 also functions as a verb meaning to reach or arrive.

parts.contribution_en: Reaching a destination or result; after a verb, marks that the action reaches its result.

guides.explanation_en: 我 is the first-person pronoun for the speaker, corresponding to “I” as a subject and “me” as an object.
兵器 means weapons or arms. 兵 supplies the association with armed conflict, while 器 contributes the sense of implements; together they refer to implements used as weapons.

parts.contribution_en: The association with armed conflict or military use.
An implement or piece of equipment.

guides.explanation_en: 旁边 refers to the area beside a person or thing. 旁 and 边 both contribute the idea of a side or edge, combining into the conventional word for a nearby side area.
guides.caveat_en: The two parts overlap in meaning; they do not mark sharply distinct zones.

parts.contribution_en: a side or edge, reinforcing the spatial sense

guides.explanation_en: 我们 means “we” or “us”: 我 refers to the speaker, and 们 marks the pronoun as plural, including other people with the speaker. Whether the listener is included depends on context.
guides.caveat_en: 们 marks plurality with pronouns and some people words; it is not a general plural ending for all nouns.

parts.contribution_en: Marks the pronoun as referring to a group.

guides.explanation_en: 来到 means to come to and reach a place or person. 来 gives movement toward a reference point, and 到 marks reaching the endpoint, making arrival explicit.
打 means to fight or attack when used of conflict with an opponent. The word names the action; its precise form depends on context.

parts.contribution_en: Names the action of fighting or attacking.

guides.explanation_en: 家 means home or household: the place where someone lives and the people associated with it.
匹 is a measure word used for counting horses. It classifies the number as a count of horses; the number and the noun identify how many there are.
说 means to express something in speech, whether by saying a brief statement or speaking at greater length. The word alone does not specify how much is said.
弟弟 is the conventional word for a younger brother, younger than a relevant person such as the speaker. The repeated form makes a single kinship term; it does not refer to two brothers.
guides.caveat_en: The younger-than relationship depends on the person being compared with.

parts.contribution_en: Contributes the kinship meaning of younger brother.
Repeats the kinship element in the conventional form; it does not add another sibling.

guides.explanation_en: 刘备 is the personal name Liu Bei, used to identify a historical figure.
guides.caveat_en: The characters function together as a name; their separate meanings do not explain the person's identity or the name's origin.

guides.explanation_en: 长矛 combines 长, “long,” with 矛, “spear.” 长 describes the spear as extended in length, giving the conventional term for a long spear.
With the reading nàn, 难 names serious trouble, hardship, or a difficult situation. It refers to the situation itself, rather than describing a task as difficult.
guides.caveat_en: This noun sense is read nàn; the same character is also read nán in other words meaning “difficult.”

parts.contribution_en: Names trouble, hardship, or a difficult situation.

guides.explanation_en: 想 expresses wanting or intending to do something. With an action following it, that action is presented as something the subject has in mind and wants to undertake.

parts.contribution_en: Expresses wanting or intending the action that follows.

guides.explanation_en: 这时 combines a demonstrative, 这, with 时, “time.” It points to a particular time already identifiable in the conversation, so it can mean “at this time” or “then.”

parts.contribution_en: Points to the particular time being referred to.
Provides the time or moment being pointed to.

guides.explanation_en: 后面 means the position or area behind something. 后 places it at the rear, and 面 contributes the sense of a side or area.

parts.contribution_en: Side or area; together, the rear side or position.

guides.explanation_en: 看到 combines looking with an achieved result: 到 marks that the looking reaches visual perception. The expression therefore means to see or notice something, rather than merely to direct one's eyes toward it.

parts.contribution_en: marks the achieved result: the looking reaches perception

guides.explanation_en: 没有 expresses that something is absent: a person does not have it, or it does not exist. 没 negates 有, which supplies the sense of having or existing.

parts.contribution_en: negates the having or existence expressed by 有

guides.explanation_en: 好 means good or pleasing, and 看 means to look at or see. Together, 好看 describes something that is pleasing to look at, hence good-looking or visually attractive.

parts.contribution_en: looking at or seeing; sets the visual aspect

guides.explanation_en: 很 intensifies an adjective, raising the stated degree of a quality. It is often translated as “very” or “quite.”

parts.contribution_en: Raises the degree of the adjective that follows.

guides.explanation_en: 桃花 means the blossoms of a peach tree. 桃 identifies the tree, and 花 names its flowers.
兄弟 literally refers to brothers, with 兄 naming an older brother and 弟 a younger brother. The pair can also refer to men joined by a brother-like bond, including sworn brothers.
guides.caveat_en: The word can name actual brothers or a brother-like relationship; it does not by itself specify which relationship is intended.

guides.explanation_en: 刀 means a knife or blade, a cutting implement that can also serve as a weapon.
黄巾军 is the proper name of the Yellow Turban army. 黄巾 provides its identifying “Yellow Turban” label, and 军 identifies the group as an army.
guides.caveat_en: The wording identifies the named group but does not explain the name's origin.

parts.contribution_en: Provides the “Yellow Turban” identifying label in the name.
Identifies the named group as an army.
